ETH.hook: Never colonised, and it keeps its own calendar — thirteen months, and about seven years behind the one the rest of the world uses.
ETH.place: The highlands of the Horn of Africa, landlocked since Eritrea broke away in 1993.
ETH.borders: The rare African borders drawn by an African power: Menelik II's conquests, confirmed in treaties with Britain, France and Italy around 1897–1908 — including the Somali-inhabited Ogaden, contested by war as late as 1977; the coast went when Eritrea left in 1993.

TZA.hook: Kilimanjaro rises 5,895m straight off the plain with no range around it — the tallest freestanding mountain on Earth.
TZA.place: On the Indian Ocean below Kenya, with Zanzibar offshore and Lake Victoria at its northwestern corner.
TZA.borders: German East Africa's lines — the 1890 Anglo-German border with Kenya famously bends around Kilimanjaro to keep the mountain on the German side — plus Zanzibar, whose 1964 union with Tanganyika coined the name Tanzania.

KEN.hook: The Great Rift Valley runs straight through it — the same crack in the continent that will eventually split Africa in two.
KEN.place: On the Indian Ocean astride the equator, between Somalia and Tanzania.
KEN.borders: British East Africa's survey lines: a straight eastern edge through Somali-inhabited country (contested at independence), Lake Victoria's waters divided by compass lines, and the Kilimanjaro bend shared with Tanzania.

MOZ.hook: One of very few country names containing all five vowels — and its coast faces Madagascar across a 400km channel.
MOZ.place: The long Indian Ocean coast below Tanzania, curving around toward South Africa.
MOZ.borders: Portugal's coastal claims, stopped from meeting Angola across the continent by Britain's 1890 ultimatum — hence the long coastal shape; the Ruvuma river draws the northern line, and the Zambezi corridor runs through the middle.

MDG.hook: Broke away from Africa about 160 million years ago, and roughly 90% of its wildlife lives nowhere else on Earth.
MDG.place: The huge island off Mozambique — the fourth largest in the world.
MDG.borders: An island 400 km off the African coast — no land border; France ruled it as one colony but attached the small Scattered Islands around it to other administrations, which is why those islets are still French and still claimed.

UGA.hook: The White Nile begins here, flowing out of Lake Victoria and then running 6,000km north to the Mediterranean.
UGA.place: Landlocked on the equator between Kenya and DR Congo, on Lake Victoria's northern shore.
UGA.borders: A British protectorate bundling old kingdoms — Buganda lends the name; the southern border follows the 1890 Anglo-German agreement's 1°S parallel, and Lake Victoria is split by straight lines through open water.

ZMB.hook: Shares Victoria Falls with Zimbabwe — the largest single sheet of falling water in the world, and its spray is visible from 50km away.
ZMB.place: Landlocked in south-central Africa above Zimbabwe, touching eight neighbours.
ZMB.borders: Rhodes's British South Africa Company concessions define it; the deep notch of the Congo Pedicle was conceded to Leopold's Congo by an 1894 agreement, and the Zambezi river gives both the southern border and the name.

SOM.hook: Has the longest coastline of any country in mainland Africa — over 3,000km wrapping around the Horn.
SOM.place: The Horn itself, curving around Ethiopia from the Gulf of Aden to the Indian Ocean.
SOM.borders: The 1960 merger of British and Italian Somalilands; the straight western line cuts through Somali grazing lands — the grievance behind the 1977 Ogaden war — and the former British north has run itself as Somaliland since 1991.

ZWE.hook: Named after Great Zimbabwe, a stone city built entirely without mortar — the largest ancient structure south of the Sahara.
ZWE.place: Landlocked between Zambia and South Africa, sharing Victoria Falls along its northern border.
ZWE.borders: The land between the rivers: Rhodes's company concessions bounded by the Limpopo in the south and the Zambezi in the north, confirmed as Southern Rhodesia's colonial limits.

MWI.hook: Lake Malawi holds more fish species than any other lake on Earth — several hundred of them found nowhere else.
MWI.place: A long thin landlocked country wrapped around its own lake, between Zambia, Tanzania and Mozambique.
MWI.borders: Britain's Nyasaland protectorate ran along the lake, and the 1890 Anglo-German agreement put the boundary on Lake Malawi's eastern shore rather than mid-water — so Malawi claims the whole lake surface, which Tanzania disputes to this day.

ERI.hook: Asmara is a near-intact Italian modernist city, built in the 1930s and now a World Heritage site.
ERI.place: On the Red Sea directly above Ethiopia — this is the coastline Ethiopia lost in 1993.
ERI.borders: Italy's Red Sea colony, delimited against Ethiopia by treaties of 1900–08 whose ambiguity at Badme helped ignite the 1998–2000 war; independence in 1993 restored the colonial outline — and took Ethiopia's entire coastline with it.

RWA.hook: The land of a thousand hills — and it banned plastic bags back in 2008, long before anyone else did.
RWA.place: Small and landlocked, between DR Congo, Uganda, Tanzania and Burundi.
RWA.borders: Unusually, a precolonial African kingdom kept nearly intact: Germany and then Belgium administered Rwanda within its royal borders, so the state matches an old polity rather than a survey line — split from twin Burundi in 1962.

BDI.hook: One of the most densely populated countries in Africa, and the southernmost headwater of the Nile rises inside it.
BDI.place: Landlocked directly below Rwanda, on the northeastern shore of Lake Tanganyika.
BDI.borders: Like Rwanda, an old kingdom whose limits survived colonization: administered under German East Africa, then Belgian Ruanda-Urundi, with the 1962 independence split restoring the two kingdoms as separate states.

DJI.hook: Lake Assal is the lowest point in Africa and one of the saltiest bodies of water anywhere — saltier than the Dead Sea.
DJI.place: A small country on the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, wedged between Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia.
DJI.borders: France's toehold at the Red Sea's exit: treaties of 1888–1901 with Ethiopia and Italy drew a small triangle around the port and the railhead — a border justified almost entirely by the railway to Addis Ababa.

MUS.hook: The dodo lived here and only here, and was gone within about eighty years of humans first landing.
MUS.place: An island in the Indian Ocean roughly 900km east of Madagascar.
MUS.borders: Volcanic islands with no neighbour for 800 km; the contested line was drawn in colonial paperwork when Britain detached the Chagos archipelago in 1965 — a severance ruled unlawful, with sovereignty finally conceded back in the 2020s.

COM.hook: Supplies most of the world's ylang-ylang — the flower essence at the heart of Chanel No. 5.
COM.place: A small archipelago in the channel between Mozambique and Madagascar.
COM.borders: A border decided by referendum, island by island: three of the four Comoro islands voted for independence in 1974, while France kept Mayotte — which Comoros claims to this day.

SYC.hook: The smallest population of any African country, and its coco de mer palm grows the largest seed in the plant kingdom.
SYC.place: 115 islands in the Indian Ocean, northeast of Madagascar.
SYC.borders: A scatter of 115 islands with no neighbours — claimed by France, taken by Britain in 1814, and independent since 1976; its only boundaries are vast maritime ones.
